context.objective: Document how we carry out KYC & Sanctions Screening, the controls and what needs confirmation.

turns.text: Usually a new investor comes in with a subscription, or something changes on an existing one, like ownership or a transfer. Then we open a KYC case for it.
Talk me through what happens in the KYC case after you open it.

We get the documents in and check them, work out who really owns the investor, then run the names through screening and if something pops up the AML reviewer looks at it. After that it gets a risk rating and someone signs off before any money is accepted.
When you check the documents, what are you comparing them against?

Mostly against the checklist of what that kind of investor needs, and against each other, so the legal names, jurisdiction and addresses line up. If something is missing or expired, we note it and ask the investor to fix it, and it stays blocked until then.
What are the investor names screened against?
Sanctions lists, SOFAC and the global ones, and we do that in Exiger. We also look at politically exposed persons and bad press on the investor, the owners and whoever controls it.
When screening produces a match, what does the AML reviewer assess and how is the result resolved?

They compare the identifiers to decide if it is a false positive or a real match, and write down the decision. If it is a false positive, we carry on, but a real or unresolved match stays blocked and goes to the compliance officer. What exactly happens after a confirmed match, like reporting? I am not sure, that has not been settled.
What guides the risk rating once the screening review is resolved?

Things like the jurisdiction, how complicated the structure is, any political exposure, sanctions links and bad press. The rating decides who has to approve and how often we review. Then the AML reviewer signs off, we tell the teams it is cleared or blocked, file the records, and it goes into ongoing monitoring.
What marks the KYC case as complete after the risk rating and sign-off?

memo_findings.answer:
Work usually starts when a new investor comes in with a subscription, or when something changes on an existing investor subscription, such as ownership or a transfer.
The usual cadence and any fixed deadline for starting or completing work have not been established.

A risk rating and sign-off follow screening, with sign-off occurring before any money is accepted.
Whether the reported sign-off, notification, filing and transition to monitoring constitute formal case closure remains to be established.
The participant reports AML reviewer sign-off, notification of teams that the case is cleared or blocked, filing of records and transition into ongoing monitoring.

A KYC case is opened for a new investor subscription or a change to an existing investor.
The role that opens the KYC case has not been identified.
The team gets and checks documents, determines who really owns the investor, and screens names. If screening produces a result, the AML reviewer looks at it; afterward the case gets a risk rating and someone signs off before money is accepted.
If a document is missing or expired, the team notes it and asks the investor to fix it; the case stays blocked until then.
The AML reviewer compares identifiers and records whether a screening match is a false positive or real. For a false positive, the team carries on; a real or unresolved match remains blocked and goes to the compliance officer.
The participant is unsure what happens after a confirmed match, including reporting, and says this has not been settled.
The risk rating takes into account jurisdiction, structural complexity, political exposure, sanctions links and bad press. The AML reviewer then signs off; the team tells teams whether the case is cleared or blocked, files records and moves it into ongoing monitoring.

The team checks the documents and screens names; an AML reviewer looks at any screening result that pops up. Someone signs off before money is accepted.
The team compares documents against the checklist for the investor type and against each other, checking that legal names, jurisdiction and addresses line up.
In Exiger, names are screened against sanctions lists, including SOFAC and global lists. The investor, its owners and whoever controls it are also checked for politically exposed person status and bad press.
The AML reviewer compares identifiers to assess a match and writes down the decision; real or unresolved matches are escalated to the compliance officer.
The AML reviewer signs off after risk rating; the rating determines who must approve. The relationship between reviewer sign-off and any other required approval has not yet been explained.

The checklist used to check documents depends on the kind of investor.
The specific document requirements that differ by investor type have not been described.
Approval responsibility and review frequency vary with the risk rating.

Investor documents are received and checked during the KYC case.
The document types and where the documents are kept have not been established.
A checklist sets out what documents the kind of investor needs and is used when checking documents.
Exiger is used to screen names against sanctions lists and to check for politically exposed persons and bad press.
The AML reviewer writes down the decision on a screening match.
The team files the case records after communicating whether the case is cleared or blocked.
The work described concerns new investors and changes to existing investor subscriptions, including ownership changes and transfers.

Sign-off is required before any money is accepted.
Document requirements are checked against the checklist for the investor type; missing or expired items block the case until fixed.
Screening covers sanctions lists, including SOFAC and global lists, as well as politically exposed persons and bad press; the participant reports that this is done in Exiger.
A false positive permits the team to carry on; a real or unresolved match remains blocked and is escalated to the compliance officer.
The risk rating determines who must approve and how often the investor is reviewed. Factors include jurisdiction, structural complexity, political exposure, sanctions links and bad press.
The rating criteria, approval levels and review frequencies associated with each rating have not been specified.
The case goes into ongoing monitoring after sign-off, communication of its cleared or blocked status and filing of records.
The participant reports using Exiger for sanctions-list screening and checks for politically exposed persons and bad press.
